The architecture I would use is a typed continuation/CFG pipeline, not a direct recursive AST-to-bytecode emitter.

In one sentence: compile Yul’s structured control effects into explicit continuations first, then compile that continuation IR into a typed symbolic stack machine, and only at the very end assemble symbolic labels into EVM byte offsets.

Yul is unusually well suited to this because its own formal description already treats statements as returning a control “mode” for break, continue, and leave; leave exits only the current Yul function, while the EVM-dialect builtin return exits the whole execution context. Yul user functions also map naturally to an EVM-style stack calling convention: arguments and a return PC are on the stack, and results are put back on the stack.

Recommended pipeline

Use these stages:

Yul AST
  -> Checked/normalized YulCore
  -> Continuation CFG / block-parameter IR
  -> Abstract typed stack machine with symbolic labels
  -> Concrete EVM bytecode via verified assembler

This staged architecture is much easier to verify than a single monolithic code generator. It mirrors the general lesson from verified compilers such as CompCert and CakeML: use intermediate languages that each remove one class of complexity, then prove semantic preservation pass by pass. CompCert’s stated correctness goal is that generated code behaves as specified by the source semantics, and CakeML’s backend explicitly uses a sequence of intermediate languages to compile high-level features away incrementally.

1. Source model: treat control effects as modes

Start with a source semantics like:

StmtResult =
  | Regular
  | Break
  | Continue
  | Leave
  | Halt(kind, args)   -- return/revert/stop/invalid/selfdestruct, etc.

Yul already has the first four as statement modes. For the EVM dialect you should extend your formal semantics with terminal modes for builtins such as return, revert, stop, and invalid, because those do not behave like Yul leave. leave returns from the current Yul function using the current values of the function’s return variables; EVM return(p, s) ends the whole execution context.

Then do not emit a runtime mode flag. That would be simple semantically but awful for gas and proofs. Instead, compile each mode to a continuation label.

Use a compilation context like this:

Kont = {
  label      : Label,
  stackShape : Shape,
  liveVars   : List Var
}

Ctx = {
  regular  : Kont,
  break    : Option Kont,
  continue : Option Kont,
  leave    : Option Kont
}

The important part is that a continuation is not just a label. It also carries the expected stack shape. Every early exit must clean up locals and temporaries before jumping.

That cleanup detail is critical for Yul, because source blocks deallocate local variables when the block exits. The source semantics restricts local state back to the variables of the enclosing block after a block completes, so a compiled early break, continue, or leave must pop any locals whose scopes are being exited.

Conceptually:

emitExit(k):
  conform currentStackShape to k.stackShape
  jump k.label

This is the central design choice.

2. Lower structured control into continuations

For every statement, compile under a context of handlers. Think of break, continue, and leave as structured exceptions, and the surrounding constructs install handlers.

if

if c { body }

lowers to:

entry:
  eval c -> tmp
  branch tmp then_label after_label

then_label:
  compile body with:
    regular  = after_label
    break    = ctx.break
    continue = ctx.continue
    leave    = ctx.leave

after_label:
  ...

No mode value is produced. A regular fallthrough reaches after_label; an early exit jumps to the relevant continuation.

switch

A switch should evaluate the selector exactly once, then branch to one case block or default. Yul explicitly has no fallthrough between cases, so each case’s regular continuation is the same join label.

eval selector -> s
if s == lit1 jump case1
if s == lit2 jump case2
...
jump default

case1:
  compile case1 with regular = join
case2:
  compile case2 with regular = join
default:
  compile default with regular = join

join:
  ...

for

For:

for { init } cond { post } { body }

generate labels:

init_entry:
  compile init with regular = cond_label

cond_label:
  eval cond -> c
  branch c body_label after_label

body_label:
  compile body with:
    regular  = post_label
    break    = after_label
    continue = post_label
    leave    = ctx.leave

post_label:
  compile post with regular = cond_label

after_label:
  ...

Yul’s continue skips to the post-iteration block, and break exits the loop. Yul also restricts break and continue to the body block of the innermost loop, not the init or update block of that same loop.

The stack-shape part matters here. Variables declared in the loop init are live in the condition, body, and post parts, but they are gone after the loop. So:

cond_label/post_label/body_label shape = outer vars + loop-init vars
after_label shape                      = outer vars only

A break from deep inside the body must pop body locals and loop-init locals before reaching after_label. A continue must pop body locals but keep loop-init locals before reaching post_label.

3. Normalize functions to a single epilogue

For each Yul function:

function f(p1, ..., pn) -> r1, ..., rm {
  body
}

compile as:

f_entry:
  bind parameters
  initialize r1, ..., rm := 0
  compile body with:
    regular = f_epilogue
    leave   = f_epilogue
    break/continue unavailable

f_epilogue:
  clean function frame
  return to caller with r1, ..., rm

This makes early return easy: leave is just a static jump to the function epilogue after cleanup.

That separation is important:

Yul leave       -> static jump to f_epilogue
function return -> dynamic jump to caller return PC
EVM return      -> terminal halt of execution context

Do not compile leave directly as a dynamic return to the caller. It should first go through the function epilogue so that return variables are gathered, locals are popped, and the function frame is restored uniformly.

Example:

function f(x) -> y {
  if iszero(x) {
    y := 1
    leave
  }
  y := add(x, 1)
}

becomes:

f_entry:
  y := 0
  c := iszero(x)
  branch c early normal

early:
  y := 1
  jump f_epilogue

normal:
  y := add(x, 1)
  jump f_epilogue

f_epilogue:
  return_to_caller(y)

This is much easier to prove than having every syntactic construct know how to return from a function.

4. Procedure calls: pass a defunctionalized return continuation

Yul functions are internal; there is no external ABI requirement for your internal calling convention. Use a simple, proved convention.

A good convention is:

callee entry expects:

  arg1 ... argn ret_pc caller_tail

using “top of stack on the left” notation.

At the call site, conceptually:

eval arguments in Yul order
push ret_label
arrange args and ret_label into callee input shape
push f_entry
JUMP

ret_label:
  -- results are now on stack
  continue caller

At the callee epilogue:

arrange stack as:

  ret_pc ret_m ... ret_1 caller_tail

JUMP

The JUMP consumes ret_pc, leaving:

ret_m ... ret_1 caller_tail

for the caller.

You must respect Yul’s specified function-call evaluation order. In the formal Yul semantics, arguments are evaluated from the last argument to the first before the callee’s fresh local state is created.

The dynamic jump proof obligation is:

ret_pc is always one of the statically generated return-continuation labels
for this callee call graph edge.

Do not model ret_pc as an arbitrary u256 in your proof. In the compiler IR, model it as a finite label value. The lowering/assembler pass then proves that each label value is encoded as the correct byte offset and points to a JUMPDEST.

This is essentially a defunctionalized continuation stack. It supports recursion naturally, because each recursive call pushes another return continuation onto the EVM stack.

5. Use a typed stack machine before raw EVM

The EVM is a stack machine with 256-bit words and a maximum stack size of 1024. But raw EVM bytecode is a poor proof target because stack layout is implicit and jumps are byte offsets.

Introduce an abstract target first:

Instr =
  | PushConst value
  | Builtin op
  | LoadLocal v
  | StoreLocal v
  | Pop
  | Dup abstract_slot
  | Swap abstract_slot
  | Jump Label
  | JumpI Label
  | Halt kind

Every block has an input stack shape:

BlockType(Label) = Shape

A block is well typed only if every terminator jumps to a label with the expected shape. This gives you a compact stack-safety theorem:

If CFG is well typed and initial stack satisfies the entry shape,
then execution never underflows the stack and every jump reaches
a valid label with the expected shape.

Only after this do you lower abstract stack operations to concrete DUPn, SWAPn, POP, PUSHn, JUMP, and JUMPI.

This also works well for Yul because the EVM dialect deliberately does not expose raw dup, swap, jump, labels, or push instructions; Yul manages local variables and control flow, so the compiler owns the low-level stack discipline.

6. Make stack shape part of every proof

The core relation between source and target should be:

Rel(layout, sourceLocals, evmStack)

meaning:

the EVM stack contains exactly the live Yul locals
according to layout, with temporary values only where
the current expression compiler says they may appear.

Then your statement correctness theorem should look like:

compileStmt(s, ctx, entry) is correct iff:

Starting from a target state related to source state (G, L),
execution from entry simulates Yul execution of s.

If Yul returns mode Regular, target reaches ctx.regular.
If Yul returns mode Break,   target reaches ctx.break.
If Yul returns mode Continue,target reaches ctx.continue.
If Yul returns mode Leave,   target reaches ctx.leave.
If Yul halts,                target halts equivalently.

At the reached continuation, the stack satisfies that
continuation's declared stack shape.

For functions:

compileFunction(f) is correct iff:

For any caller stack tail and any valid return continuation k,
starting at f_entry with args + k + caller_tail simulates
Yul function execution from fresh function locals.

On regular fallthrough or leave, execution jumps to k with
the return values on top of the unchanged caller_tail.

On EVM-level halt, execution halts with the same observable effect.

This theorem should be parametric in the caller tail. That parametricity is what proves frame isolation.

Use small-step semantics or a fuel-indexed semantics for the interprocedural theorem, especially if you support recursion and loops. A pure terminating big-step theorem is not enough to express divergence or out-of-gas behavior cleanly.

7. Be careful with memory spills

For a verified Yul-to-EVM compiler, avoid using EVM memory as a general spill area unless you have a verified memory-safety condition.

Yul programs can call mload, mstore, keccak256, return, revert, and call-like builtins over memory. Compiler locals stored in memory can become observable. Solidity’s Yul tooling has a memoryguard(size) mechanism: the program promises it uses only [0, size) or memory starting at a returned pointer, and the optimizer may use [size, ptr) for tasks such as moving otherwise unreachable stack variables to memory.

For a first verified compiler, I would make stack allocation partial:

compile(P) =
  | Some bytecode, with proof of semantic preservation
  | None, if stack layout/accessibility fails

That is acceptable for a verified compiler: the theorem says that whenever the compiler succeeds, the output is correct.

Later you can add a verified memory-spilling pass under an explicit memoryguard or “memory-safe Yul” assumption.

8. Handle verbatim separately

Yul’s verbatim can inject arbitrary bytecode and can break stack and control-flow assumptions. The Solidity docs warn that the compiler assumes a specified input/output stack effect and that violating restrictions can lead to undefined behavior; restrictions include not jumping into or out of verbatim blocks and not accessing stack contents beyond declared inputs/outputs.

For formal verification, choose one:

1. Reject verbatim.
2. Treat verbatim as an opaque primitive with a verified contract.
3. Require the user to supply a proof/certificate for each verbatim block.

Do not silently allow arbitrary verbatim bytecode in the verified subset.

9. Label resolution and assembler proof

Keep labels symbolic until the last pass.

The final assembler should prove:

resolve(label) points to a JUMPDEST
all static jumps target valid labels
all dynamic return labels are drawn from a finite allowed set
PUSH width is sufficient for the resolved byte offset
assembled code preserves symbolic execution semantics

This gives you a clean split:

CFG correctness theorem:
  about labels and continuations

Assembler theorem:
  labels become concrete byte offsets correctly

Do not mix these in one proof.

10. Legacy EVM vs EOF

For today’s ordinary EVM bytecode, use the explicit return-PC convention above. If you intentionally target EOF-style EVM, the architecture still applies, but the final lowering changes: EOF proposals include static relative jumps, functions, stack validation, and JUMPF/non-returning functions. EIP-7692 is listed as a stagnant meta EIP at the time of the cited EIP page, so I would not make EOF the default target unless your deployment environment explicitly supports it.

The main recommendation

Use this invariant throughout:

Every label has a declared stack shape.
Every control transfer must conform to the target shape.
Every source control mode maps to a continuation.
Every function has one epilogue.
Every procedure return uses a verified return-continuation value.

That gives you a compiler architecture where conditionals, loops, break, continue, leave, recursion, and multi-return functions are all handled by the same mechanism: continuations plus stack-shape typing.

Oh wait, before you do that, here's a possible issue that needs to be fixed in the PR, can you verify:

[P1] No-default switch is still semantically wrong through the Yul notation layer. EvmYul/Yul/YulNotation.lean (line 275) translates an omitted default to [.Break]. With the PR’s new switch execution in EvmYul/Yul/Interpreter.lean (line 654), a no-match switch with no default executes break instead of doing nothing. Solidity’s Yul spec says switch-without-default is equivalent to an empty default, and only the matching/default branch is taken: Solidity Yul docs. I confirmed locally with a scratch probe:
parsed switch no default/no match: break
direct AST empty default/no match: regular
This can incorrectly break out of loops or leave a checkpoint where Yul should continue regularly. Fix: translate .none default to [], and add a regression test for switch 1 case 2 {}.

```

FYI, here is a memo from ChatGPT Pro after doing some more research. Pro does not know exactly what you are working on, so it's fine if you already are on this track or if you think you have a better one. Take it for what it's worth.

Research steering memo: optimized search for an M23 polynomial over Q

Current status:
Do not claim the M23 inverse Galois problem over Q is solved. As of the current literature/database check, M23 remains open over Q. Zywina’s latest small-simple-groups list still includes M23 among unresolved simple groups of order < 10^8; the Klüners–Malle database states that all transitive groups up to degree 23 are represented except M23; and the database’s missing-polynomials page lists 23T5 as the sole missing degree-23 group.

Main conclusion:
The search should be certificate-first and Hurwitz-component-first. The most promising computational program is not a blind polynomial search. Build a high-performance exact M23/Hurwitz engine, use it to reproduce known braid-orbit data, incorporate recent field-of-definition theory for components, and then use optimized orbit/candidate searches to locate a low-genus or otherwise arithmetically usable component over Q.

Priority sources and why they matter:
1. ATLAS / GAP CTblLib M23 data.
   - Use this as trusted input for the degree-23 permutation representation, conjugacy classes, cycle types, maximal subgroups, and validation.
   - M23 has order 10,200,960 and 17 conjugacy classes.
   - Maximal subgroups listed in CTblLib: M22, L3(4).2_2, 2^4:A7, A8, M11, 2^4:(3 x A5).2, and 23:11.
   - The ATLAS degree-23 representation is primitive, 4-transitive, has point stabilizer M22, and acts on the Steiner system S(4,7,23).

2. Häfner 2022, “Braid orbits and the Mathieu group M23 as Galois group.”
   - This is the core roadmap for finite braid-orbit computations.
   - Häfner says no polynomial in Z[x] with Galois group M23 is known and M23/Q remains open.
   - Three-point rational class vectors for M23 do not appear to solve the problem.
   - The B4 action for (3A)^4 was computed completely.
   - The open heavy computations are:
     B4((5A)^4, 30400),
     B4((6A)^4, 72528),
     B4((8A)^4, 198488).
   - Häfner explicitly says these computations are parallelizable and could either rule out these class vectors or reveal small B4-orbits useful for geometric realizations over Q(v,t).

3. Seguin 2023, “Fields of Definition of Components of Hurwitz Spaces.”
   - This is a major strategic update.
   - Seguin proves the existence of components defined over Q for connected M23-covers with only four branch points.
   - The construction uses the fact that M23 is generated by two conjugate order-3 elements. He gives explicit permutations a and b in GAP syntax and verifies StructureDescription(Group(a,b)) = "M23" and IsConjugate(Group(a,b),a,b) = true.
   - This does not itself give a rational point or an explicit polynomial, but it changes what the search engine should look for: not merely rational class vectors, but concrete B4 components with field-of-definition data and rationality/genus information.
   - Codex should implement field-of-definition/component invariants, not only orbit size.

4. Elkies 2010, “The complex polynomials P(x) with Gal(P(x)-t) ≅ M23.”
   - This gives known degree-23 polynomial covers with monodromy M23, but over a quartic coefficient field, not Q.
   - The relevant three-point branch cycle structure is order 23 at infinity and orders 2 and 4 at the other branch points.
   - Elkies notes that there are four M23 covers up to equivalence, while many A23 covers have the same cycle structure.
   - This is a high-value validation/descent target: reproduce its cycle data, factorization tests, and perhaps attempt field-of-definition descent/twisting, but do not expect a direct Q-polynomial from this alone.

5. Van Bommel–Costa–Elkies–Keller–Schiavone–Voight 2025, 17T7 paper.
   - This solved the other notorious small-degree transitive case using a mod-2 Galois representation attached to a Hilbert modular form and reconstructed an explicit degree-17 polynomial.
   - The paper explicitly describes M23 as the remaining notorious degree ≤ 23 case.
   - This suggests a longer-term Galois-representation route for M23, but it is not the first implementation priority.

6. Conway–McKay–Trojan / Abhyankar positive-characteristic examples.
   - M23 occurs over F2(t), for example via x^23 + x^3 + t in characteristic 2.
   - This does not solve the Q problem, but it is relevant to possible mod-2/Golay-code or additive-polynomial inspiration.
   - Treat this as a speculative research track, not a primary computational target.

Revised project priorities:

Phase A: exact M23 backend and certificates
- Load/generate the ATLAS degree-23 permutation representation.
- Verify order 10,200,960.
- Verify all 17 conjugacy classes and cycle types.
- Export machine-readable class data.
- Export maximal subgroup data from GAP/CTblLib/Magma.
- Build the maximal-subgroup generation sieve:
  a tuple generates M23 iff no maximal-subgroup conjugate contains all tuple entries.
- Validate generation sieve against GAP on random tuples.

Phase B: reproduce known braid-orbit data
- Implement B4 action using Häfner’s convention and document the convention.
- Reproduce product-one Nielsen class sizes and orbit sizes where feasible.
- First full M23 target: reproduce (3A)^4.
  Expected from Häfner:
    li((3A)^4) = 37,296.
    B4 action was computed completely.
    Table 9.2 records two orbit sizes 8,316 and 28,980, with high braid genera.
- Use (3A)^4 as the main benchmark because it is small enough to complete and directly connected to Seguin’s order-3 generator construction.

Phase C: integrate Seguin’s four-branch-point component result
- Add a module `component_field_of_definition`.
- Implement the explicit order-3 permutations from Seguin Example 5.5:
    a := (1,22,14)(2,13,9)(3,8,6)(7,16,21)(10,18,19)(11,23,12)
    b := (2,4,16)(3,5,7)(6,11,12)(8,9,14)(10,21,20)(15,18,17)
  Convert to zero-based indexing internally if needed.
- Verify:
    order(a) = order(b) = 3
    Group(a,b) = M23
    a and b are conjugate in M23
- Construct tuples of the form:
    (a, a^-1, b, b^-1)
  and more generally:
    (a, a^-1, a^gamma, (a^-1)^gamma)
  where <a, a^gamma> = M23.
- Classify which B4 orbit each such tuple belongs to in (3A)^4.
- Determine whether the relevant orbit is unique by size/genus and therefore Galois-stable.
- Compute symmetrized orbit data and braid genus.
- Important: Seguin’s result is about field of definition of components, not existence of rational points. Do not overclaim.

Phase D: use field-of-definition theory to guide new searches
Instead of only scanning symmetric vectors, scan “Seguin-style” tuples:
  (g, g^-1, h, h^-1)
where:
  g and h are conjugate or power-conjugate where appropriate,
  <g,h> = M23,
  orders are in {2,3,4,6} where Seguin’s general examples apply,
  the resulting class vector is rationally stable,
  the B4 orbit has small size and low braid genus.

Search classes:
- (3A)^4: fully reproduce and analyze; likely high genus, so probably not directly useful for rational points, but essential validation.
- (4A)^4: Häfner mostly rules out because known small orbits have high genus.
- (5A)^4, (6A)^4, (8A)^4: run Häfner’s open capped searches after engine validation.
- mixed pairs:
    (C,C,D,D)
    (C,C,D,D) with entries as (g,g^-1,h,h^-1)
  where C,D are rational or Galois-paired classes and where Riemann-Hurwitz genus is favorable.

Phase E: attack Häfner’s open computations
Implement optimized enumeration for:
  B4((5A)^4, 30400)
  B4((6A)^4, 72528)
  B4((8A)^4, 198488)

Use:
- fixed-first-entry normalization,
- quotient by centralizer,
- maximal-subgroup generation sieve,
- pair-product joins,
- sharded hash-based orbit enumeration,
- exact deterministic packed states,
- optional GPU acceleration only for pair products, frontier expansion, sorting/deduplication.

Do not GPU-accelerate GAP. Build exact custom kernels and recheck every result on CPU/GAP.

Phase F: descent tracks
1. Elkies quartic-field M23 covers:
   - Reproduce the branch cycle structure (2A,4A,23A/B).
   - Reproduce factorization/cycle-type tests.
   - Study Galois conjugates of the four covers.
   - Test whether any twist/descent to Q is visible.
   - Use as validation for the polynomial/cycle-type verifier.

2. Häfner quadratic-field covers:
   - Reconstruct covers over Q(sqrt(-7))(v,t) and Q(sqrt(-15))(v,t) with class vectors (14A,2A,2A,2A) and (15A,2A,2A,2A).
   - Test descent or specialization-to-Q strategies.
   - Record failures honestly.

Phase G: direct polynomial sieve as secondary path
- Build a modular factor-pattern sieve for degree-23 integer polynomials.
- Required filters:
    irreducible over Q,
    square discriminant,
    all good-prime factorization patterns among M23 cycle types,
    at least one Frobenius 23-cycle,
    at least one Frobenius class not contained in 23:11 once Gal <= M23 is known.
- This is not a blind search. It should consume candidates generated by covers, descent attempts, or structured local ramification templates.
- Final certificate must prove Gal(f) <= M23 using a Stauduhar/resolvent/Witt-design method and then prove equality with Frobenius data plus maximal-subgroup exclusion.

Immediate next implementation tasks:
1. Add `docs/research_update_YYYYMMDD.md` summarizing:
   - M23 still open over Q.
   - Häfner open B4 computations.
   - Seguin four-branch-point Q-component result.
   - Elkies quartic-field covers.
   - 17T7 Galois-representation precedent.

2. Add `scripts/seguin_m23_order3_pair.gap`:
   - define a,b from Seguin;
   - verify orders, generated group, conjugacy;
   - export a,b, class IDs, and tuple (a,a^-1,b,b^-1).

3. Add `src/component_fod/`:
   - rational class/multidiscriminant checks;
   - power-conjugacy/Galois action on classes;
   - component field-of-definition flags;
   - Seguin-style tuple generator.

4. Add `tests/test_seguin_pair.*`:
   - order(a)=order(b)=3;
   - generated group is M23;
   - tuple is product-one;
   - tuple generates M23;
   - tuple lies in class vector (3A)^4;
   - braid orbit classification agrees with reproduced (3A)^4 data.

5. Add `benchmarks/benchmark_3A4.*`:
   - reproduce li((3A)^4)=37,296;
   - reproduce the two B4 orbit sizes reported by Häfner;
   - profile normalization, generation sieve, and braid frontier expansion.

6. Only after that, run large open searches for (5A)^4, (6A)^4, and (8A)^4.

Critical cautions:
- A component defined over Q is not the same as a Q-rational point on the component.
- A rational class vector is not the same as a rational component.
- A small braid orbit is not automatically useful unless the associated Hurwitz curve/component has accessible rational points.
- A polynomial passing many Frobenius cycle tests is not a proof of Gal(f)=M23.
- GPU output must be treated as untrusted until exact CPU/GAP verification.

Here is some general architectural advice from an oracle. Is this what we do?

The best organization is to **make control flow carry an explicit stack contract**, rather than trying to recover stack shape from generated EVM jumps after the fact.

In practice: treat every `break`, `continue`, `leave`, and halting `return(...)` as an **effect** with a known target stack shape, and make code generation prove locally that it either falls through with the normal shape or transfers control after restoring the target shape.

One useful framing is:

```text
compileStmt Γ K stmt
```

where:

```text
Γ = current local-variable stack layout
K = control context:
    break    ↦ target label + required stack shape
    continue ↦ target label + required stack shape
    leave    ↦ function-exit label + required stack shape
```

Then the invariant is:

```text
A compiled statement starting in shape Γ either:

1. falls through normally with the expected Γ',
2. jumps to K.break    with exactly K.break.shape,
3. jumps to K.continue with exactly K.continue.shape,
4. jumps to K.leave    with exactly K.leave.shape,
5. halts the EVM execution.
```

This mirrors Yul’s own semantic structure: the official Yul specification models statement execution as returning a mode such as regular, `break`, `continue`, or `leave`; blocks also restrict the local state back to the variables visible at block entry. ([Solidity Documentation][1])

A few concrete recommendations.

### 1. Separate `leave` from EVM `return`

Yul’s structured function return is `leave`. It exits the current Yul function and returns the current values of the declared return variables. The EVM-dialect builtin `return(offset, size)` is different: it terminates the whole EVM execution context. ([Solidity Documentation][1])

So model them as different effects:

```text
leave               : structured function exit
return(offset,size) : EVM halt, no successor stack shape
revert(offset,size) : EVM halt/revert, no successor stack shape
stop                : EVM halt, no successor stack shape
```

Do **not** try to give EVM `RETURN` a continuation stack shape. It has none.

### 2. Give every label an arity/shape

Treat EVM labels like typed join points:

```text
Label L_post       expects shape Π · loop_vars
Label L_after_loop expects shape Π · outer_vars
Label L_fun_exit   expects shape Π · return_pc · return_values
```

Then every `JUMP`/`JUMPI` proof obligation becomes:

```text
before jumping to L:
    normalize current stack to shape expected by L
    push L
    JUMP
```

Remember that the jump destination itself is consumed by `JUMP`, so your typed-assembler spec should account for:

```text
before JUMP: expected_target_shape · dest
after JUMPDEST: expected_target_shape
```

The important thing is that **the label owns the shape**. You do not want each predecessor to have its own interpretation of the stack at the join.

This is similar to SSA block parameters or WebAssembly block result types: control-flow targets have explicit input contracts.

### 3. Use a “statement baseline” discipline

Make expressions and statements have different stack rules.

For expressions:

```text
compileExpr Γ e : Γ ↦ Γ · values(e)
```

For statements:

```text
compileStmt Γ stmt : Γ ↦ Γ'
```

with the discipline that **no expression temporaries survive statement boundaries**.

Yul already has a useful restriction here: expressions used as statements must evaluate to zero values, ordinary expression positions must evaluate to one value, and multi-value expressions are only allowed in declarations or assignments. ([Solidity Documentation][1])

This gives you simple rules:

```text
if cond { body }

1. compile cond: Γ ↦ Γ · cond
2. consume cond for JUMPI
3. true branch starts in Γ
4. false branch starts in Γ
5. both branches join at Γ
```

For `switch`, do the same: evaluate the scrutinee, consume it along each dispatch path, and require every case body to fall through or exit with the same target contracts.

### 4. Model block exit as stack-region unwinding

Yul locals are naturally stack allocated: the official docs describe a fresh stack slot for a local variable and automatic removal at block end. ([Solidity Documentation][1])

Exploit that. Treat a block as creating a stack region:

```text
entry shape:     Π
inside block:    Π · locals
normal exit:     pop locals, return to Π
break exit:      pop locals, then jump to K.break
continue exit:   pop locals, then jump to K.continue
leave exit:      pop locals, then jump to K.leave
```

The key abstraction is a reusable operation:

```text
unwind(current_shape, target_shape)
```

with one proof:

```text
unwind preserves the prefix Π and removes/rearranges only the region that is dead at the exit.
```

Then `break`, `continue`, and `leave` do not contain bespoke stack reasoning. They call the same proven unwinder.

You can implement this either inline:

```text
POP
POP
PUSH L_break
JUMP
```

or with cleanup landing pads:

```text
break inside block:
    JUMP L_block_break_cleanup

L_block_break_cleanup:
    pop block locals
    JUMP outer break target
```

For verification, cleanup landing pads are often nicer because each scope has one local proof for each escaping effect.

### 5. Treat loops as installing two local continuations

For a Yul loop:

```yul
for { init } cond { post } {
    body
}
```

install a loop control frame:

```text
continue ↦ L_post
break    ↦ L_after_loop
leave    ↦ inherited function-exit target
```

Yul’s `break` and `continue` are restricted to the body of the relevant loop, and `continue` skips to the post part; the condition must evaluate to one value. ([Solidity Documentation][1])

A good stack-shape organization is:

```text
outer shape:        Π
after init:         Π · loop_init_vars

L_cond expects:     Π · loop_init_vars
L_body expects:     Π · loop_init_vars
L_post expects:     Π · loop_init_vars
L_after_loop expects Π
```

Then:

```text
continue from body:
    pop body-local variables
    jump L_post
    -- preserves loop_init_vars

break from body:
    pop body-local variables
    pop loop_init_vars
    jump L_after_loop

normal body fallthrough:
    pop body-local variables
    jump L_post

normal loop termination:
    pop loop_init_vars
    fall through at L_after_loop
```

Be especially careful with variables declared in the `init` block. Yul’s scoping rule says the init scope extends through the condition, post, and body, and `for { I... } C { P... } { B... }` is equivalent to `{ I... for {} C { P... } { B... } }` for scoping purposes. ([Solidity Documentation][1])

That means `continue` preserves init variables, while `break` leaves the whole loop scope.

### 6. Compile `leave` through a single function epilogue

For each Yul function, create one function-exit label:

```text
L_fun_exit expects: function-frame-shape
```

Every `leave` should unwind to that label. The epilogue is the only place that implements the function calling convention:

```text
L_fun_exit:
    arrange return values in caller-expected order
    remove callee locals/arguments
    jump to return_pc
```

Yul functions in the EVM dialect take arguments and a return PC from the stack and put results back on the stack; return variables are assigned inside the function, and `leave` returns whatever values are currently assigned to them. ([Solidity Documentation][1])

So prove the calling convention once:

```text
function epilogue theorem:
    given a well-formed callee frame,
    executing L_fun_exit returns control to return_pc
    with exactly the declared return values on the caller stack.
```

Then each individual `leave` proof is just:

```text
current stack shape
  -- unwind locals
  -- preserve/copy return variables
  -- jump L_fun_exit
```

### 7. Make the type of compiled code mention all possible exits

A compact formal judgment could look like this:

```text
Γ ; K ⊢ stmt ⇝ code : Γ'
```

meaning:

```text
If execution starts with stack layout Γ, then code either:

- falls through with Γ',
- exits via break with K.break.shape,
- exits via continue with K.continue.shape,
- exits via leave with K.leave.shape,
- halts.
```

For blocks, extend `K` with cleanup wrappers:

```text
compileBlock Γ K { s1 ... sn }:

    Γ_block = Γ plus block locals

    K_block.break    = cleanup(block locals); K.break
    K_block.continue = cleanup(block locals); K.continue
    K_block.leave    = cleanup(block locals); K.leave

    compile statements under K_block

    on normal fallthrough:
        cleanup(block locals)
```

This directly matches the Yul semantic idea that abrupt modes propagate until consumed by a loop/function boundary. The docs’ formal semantics for loops consumes `break`, treats `leave` as propagating, and routes ordinary/continue-like flow through the post block. ([Solidity Documentation][1])

### 8. Prove a small typed-assembler layer first

Do not prove stack-shape preservation directly over raw byte arrays. Use a small typed assembly IR:

```text
instrSpec(PUSH x)  : S ↦ S · x
instrSpec(POP)     : S · x ↦ S
instrSpec(DUP i)   : S ↦ S · S[i]
instrSpec(SWAP i)  : ...
instrSpec(JUMP L)  : shape(L) · L ↦ jumps_to L with shape(L)
instrSpec(JUMPI L) : shape(L) · cond · L ↦ either jumps_to L with shape(L) or falls through shape(L)
```

Then have a final assembler pass erase labels and prove that label addresses are valid `JUMPDEST`s.

This gives you two independent proof layers:

```text
Yul → typed stack CFG:
    preserves Yul control semantics and stack contracts

typed stack CFG → EVM bytecode:
    preserves instruction-level EVM behavior and jump validity
```

Yul was deliberately designed with high-level control constructs and without explicit `SWAP`, `DUP`, `JUMPDEST`, `JUMP`, or `JUMPI` statements because those obscure data/control flow; leaning into a structured intermediate proof layer fits that design goal. ([Solidity Documentation][1])

### 9. Delay clever stack-slot reuse

For the first verified compiler, avoid proving liveness-based early slot freeing at the same time as control flow. Use lexical stack regions first:

```text
let x := ...
...
end of lexical block: pop x
```

The Solidity docs note that optimized Yul/EVM compilation may free slots after last use, but that is an optimization choice. ([Solidity Documentation][1])

For a verified compiler, make early freeing a separate pass:

```text
Yul
 → lexical-stack IR        -- simple proof
 → liveness-optimized IR   -- separate slot-reuse proof
 → typed assembly
 → EVM
```

Trying to combine control-flow unwinding, return handling, and last-use slot reuse in one correctness theorem is usually where these proofs become painful.

### A small example

Suppose you compile:

```yul
{
    let x := 0
    for { let i := 0 } lt(i, 10) { i := add(i, 1) } {
        if eq(i, 5) { break }
        if eq(i, 7) { continue }
        x := add(x, i)
    }
}
```

Use shapes like:

```text
Π                     outer unknown prefix
Π · x                 after declaring x
Π · x · i             inside loop scope
```

Then labels get contracts:

```text
L_cond       expects Π · x · i
L_body       expects Π · x · i
L_post       expects Π · x · i
L_after_loop expects Π · x
L_after_blk  expects Π
```

Control exits inside the body are compiled as:

```text
break:
    normalize to Π · x · i
    pop i
    jump L_after_loop

continue:
    normalize to Π · x · i
    jump L_post

end of block:
    pop x
    fall through with Π
```

If the body had local variables, for example:

```yul
{
    let t := add(x, i)
    if eq(t, 5) { continue }
}
```

then the `continue` path first pops `t`, restoring `Π · x · i`, and only then jumps to `L_post`.

### The core rule

The guiding rule I would use is:

> **Every syntactic construct owns the stack slots it introduces, and every control-flow edge leaving that construct must run its cleanup before reaching the target continuation.**

Equivalently:

```text
break/continue/leave should not be “jumps”.
They should be “unwind to a typed continuation”.
```

That organization keeps the hard proof obligations small:

```text
expression compiler preserves Γ and pushes exactly n values
statement compiler restores Γ on normal fallthrough
block compiler unwinds its local region on every exit
loop compiler installs break/continue continuations
function compiler installs one leave continuation
typed assembler enforces label stack shapes
```

Once those lemmas exist, stack shape for `break`, `continue`, `leave`, and function return becomes mostly compositional instead of a whole-program CFG argument.

[1]: https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/yul.html "Yul — Solidity 0.8.36-develop documentation"

Please set a goal to do that rewrite before anything else. Here is the design, put it in an md file so that you remember it.

The best organization is to **make control flow carry an explicit stack contract**, rather than trying to recover stack shape from generated EVM jumps after the fact.

In practice: treat every break, continue, leave, and halting return(...) as an **effect** with a known target stack shape, and make code generation prove locally that it either falls through with the normal shape or transfers control after restoring the target shape.

One useful framing is:
text
compileStmt Γ K stmt

where:
text
Γ = current local-variable stack layout
K = control context:
    break    ↦ target label + required stack shape
    continue ↦ target label + required stack shape
    leave    ↦ function-exit label + required stack shape

Then the invariant is:
text
A compiled statement starting in shape Γ either:

1. falls through normally with the expected Γ',
2. jumps to K.break    with exactly K.break.shape,
3. jumps to K.continue with exactly K.continue.shape,
4. jumps to K.leave    with exactly K.leave.shape,
5. halts the EVM execution.

This mirrors Yul’s own semantic structure: the official Yul specification models statement execution as returning a mode such as regular, break, continue, or leave; blocks also restrict the local state back to the variables visible at block entry. ([Solidity Documentation][1])

A few concrete recommendations.

### 1. Separate leave from EVM return

Yul’s structured function return is leave. It exits the current Yul function and returns the current values of the declared return variables. The EVM-dialect builtin return(offset, size) is different: it terminates the whole EVM execution context. ([Solidity Documentation][1])

So model them as different effects:
text
leave               : structured function exit
return(offset,size) : EVM halt, no successor stack shape
revert(offset,size) : EVM halt/revert, no successor stack shape
stop                : EVM halt, no successor stack shape

Do **not** try to give EVM RETURN a continuation stack shape. It has none.

### 2. Give every label an arity/shape

Treat EVM labels like typed join points:
text
Label L_post       expects shape Π · loop_vars
Label L_after_loop expects shape Π · outer_vars
Label L_fun_exit   expects shape Π · return_pc · return_values

Then every JUMP/JUMPI proof obligation becomes:
text
before jumping to L:
    normalize current stack to shape expected by L
    push L
    JUMP

Remember that the jump destination itself is consumed by JUMP, so your typed-assembler spec should account for:
text
before JUMP: expected_target_shape · dest
after JUMPDEST: expected_target_shape

The important thing is that **the label owns the shape**. You do not want each predecessor to have its own interpretation of the stack at the join.

This is similar to SSA block parameters or WebAssembly block result types: control-flow targets have explicit input contracts.

### 3. Use a “statement baseline” discipline

Make expressions and statements have different stack rules.

For expressions:
text
compileExpr Γ e : Γ ↦ Γ · values(e)

For statements:
text
compileStmt Γ stmt : Γ ↦ Γ'

with the discipline that **no expression temporaries survive statement boundaries**.

Yul already has a useful restriction here: expressions used as statements must evaluate to zero values, ordinary expression positions must evaluate to one value, and multi-value expressions are only allowed in declarations or assignments. ([Solidity Documentation][1])

This gives you simple rules:
text
if cond { body }

1. compile cond: Γ ↦ Γ · cond
2. consume cond for JUMPI
3. true branch starts in Γ
4. false branch starts in Γ
5. both branches join at Γ

For switch, do the same: evaluate the scrutinee, consume it along each dispatch path, and require every case body to fall through or exit with the same target contracts.

### 4. Model block exit as stack-region unwinding

Yul locals are naturally stack allocated: the official docs describe a fresh stack slot for a local variable and automatic removal at block end. ([Solidity Documentation][1])

Exploit that. Treat a block as creating a stack region:
text
entry shape:     Π
inside block:    Π · locals
normal exit:     pop locals, return to Π
break exit:      pop locals, then jump to K.break
continue exit:   pop locals, then jump to K.continue
leave exit:      pop locals, then jump to K.leave

The key abstraction is a reusable operation:
text
unwind(current_shape, target_shape)

with one proof:
text
unwind preserves the prefix Π and removes/rearranges only the region that is dead at the exit.

Then break, continue, and leave do not contain bespoke stack reasoning. They call the same proven unwinder.

You can implement this either inline:
text
POP
POP
PUSH L_break
JUMP

or with cleanup landing pads:
text
break inside block:
    JUMP L_block_break_cleanup

L_block_break_cleanup:
    pop block locals
    JUMP outer break target

For verification, cleanup landing pads are often nicer because each scope has one local proof for each escaping effect.

### 5. Treat loops as installing two local continuations

For a Yul loop:
yul
for { init } cond { post } {
    body
}

install a loop control frame:
text
continue ↦ L_post
break    ↦ L_after_loop
leave    ↦ inherited function-exit target

Yul’s break and continue are restricted to the body of the relevant loop, and continue skips to the post part; the condition must evaluate to one value. ([Solidity Documentation][1])

A good stack-shape organization is:
text
outer shape:        Π
after init:         Π · loop_init_vars

L_cond expects:     Π · loop_init_vars
L_body expects:     Π · loop_init_vars
L_post expects:     Π · loop_init_vars
L_after_loop expects Π

Then:
text
continue from body:
    pop body-local variables
    jump L_post
    -- preserves loop_init_vars

break from body:
    pop body-local variables
    pop loop_init_vars
    jump L_after_loop

normal body fallthrough:
    pop body-local variables
    jump L_post

normal loop termination:
    pop loop_init_vars
    fall through at L_after_loop

Be especially careful with variables declared in the init block. Yul’s scoping rule says the init scope extends through the condition, post, and body, and for { I... } C { P... } { B... } is equivalent to { I... for {} C { P... } { B... } } for scoping purposes. ([Solidity Documentation][1])

That means continue preserves init variables, while break leaves the whole loop scope.

### 6. Compile leave through a single function epilogue

For each Yul function, create one function-exit label:
text
L_fun_exit expects: function-frame-shape

Every leave should unwind to that label. The epilogue is the only place that implements the function calling convention:
text
L_fun_exit:
    arrange return values in caller-expected order
    remove callee locals/arguments
    jump to return_pc

Yul functions in the EVM dialect take arguments and a return PC from the stack and put results back on the stack; return variables are assigned inside the function, and leave returns whatever values are currently assigned to them. ([Solidity Documentation][1])

So prove the calling convention once:
text
function epilogue theorem:
    given a well-formed callee frame,
    executing L_fun_exit returns control to return_pc
    with exactly the declared return values on the caller stack.

Then each individual leave proof is just:
text
current stack shape
  -- unwind locals
  -- preserve/copy return variables
  -- jump L_fun_exit

### 7. Make the type of compiled code mention all possible exits

A compact formal judgment could look like this:
text
Γ ; K ⊢ stmt ⇝ code : Γ'

meaning:
text
If execution starts with stack layout Γ, then code either:

- falls through with Γ',
- exits via break with K.break.shape,
- exits via continue with K.continue.shape,
- exits via leave with K.leave.shape,
- halts.

For blocks, extend K with cleanup wrappers:

    K_block.break    = cleanup(block locals); K.break
    K_block.continue = cleanup(block locals); K.continue
    K_block.leave    = cleanup(block locals); K.leave

    compile statements under K_block

    on normal fallthrough:
        cleanup(block locals)

# Verifiable Compiler

Use this skill for Lean-first verified compiler work. The primary artifacts are
Lean definitions, compiler functions, semantics, relations, and checked
theorems. Tests, fixtures, docs, oracle advice, and external tools are support
evidence only.

The default shape is: start near
the target, add one semantic abstraction layer at a time, prove the adjacent
lowering completely for the source language in scope, then move up.

## Start Or Resume

1. Inspect local state before planning:
   - `git status --short` (if this is not a git repo, initialize with a commit);
   - `lakefile.lean`, `lean-toolchain`, root modules, theorem files, tests, and
     recent build scripts;
   - `ROADMAP.md` and `PROGRESS_LOG.md`, if present.
2. Call `get_goal`. If no active goal exists, create one whose objective
   matches the user's concrete request in this turn. For sustained build
   requests, include the requested compiler scope and the end-to-end theorem
   standard. For narrower work, keep the objective scoped to that audit,
   proof-debugging, refactor, architecture review, skill edit, or pass-specific
   task.
3. When starting or resuming sustained verified-compiler work, say explicitly
   that this workflow is using `$verifiable-compiler`, and remind the user
   that future continuation requests should mention `$verifiable-compiler`.
   Do this at start/resume or handoff, not in every status update.
4. Use exactly two project docs by default:
   - `ROADMAP.md`: sparse checklist and current public spine.
   - `PROGRESS_LOG.md`: flat timestamped log of proofs, tests, bottlenecks,
     architecture risks, deletions, oracle IDs, and status.
5. Every time the agent restarts from conversation compaction, append a short
   timestamped `PROGRESS_LOG.md` entry before continuing, including for narrow
   follow-up tasks. Name it as a compaction resume, summarize the current
   objective/checkpoint in one sentence, and keep it concise.
6. Do not create feature matrices, trust ledgers, design histories, or incident
   reports unless the user asks. If legacy docs exist, read them as context but
   do not keep adding synchronized truth there.

## Git Checkpoints

- Commit verified checkpoints as you go. After a meaningful theorem, boundary
  cleanup, refactor, or audit passes its relevant build/axiom checks, create a
  focused git commit before starting the next substantial proof thread.
- Keep commits honest: include only project files that belong to the verified
  checkpoint, and mention the Lean build or axiom audit that passed. Do not
  commit huge build logs, scratch outputs, or unrelated generated clutter.
- If the user says all current work belongs to the agent, treat the dirty tree
  as owned work for staging purposes, while still keeping commits coherent and
  avoiding accidental inclusion of temporary logs or secrets.

For a broad build request, the goal is not complete until concrete Lean theorem
statements connect every source-language feature in scope to the declared target
interpreter. Do not silently reinterpret a request for a source language as a
request for a convenient accepted fragment.

For any active goal that asks to complete a layer or compiler pass, do not stop
while the public theorem still takes compiler-generated evidence as an
unproved input. Treat these as blockers, not residual assumptions: generated
layout records, compilation certificates, replay certificates, whole-program
call or callee-preservation obligations, return-layout obligations, generated
label/token uniqueness tables, and proof-carrying emitted-code segments. It is
acceptable to expose fundamental semantic or resource premises such as source
acceptedness, input run/evaluation, initial-state relation, fuel/gas bounds, or
explicit code-size/no-overflow bounds, but any compiler artifact that can be
computed from the source program must either be constructed by a checked Lean
theorem or remain an explicitly unfinished goal.

## Core Strategy

Build a target-up semantic tower, one complete layer at a time:

1. Choose or define the declared target interpreter and observation model.
2. Define the lowest useful layer above that target.
3. Add exactly one real semantic abstraction in the next higher layer.
4. Give that layer syntax, semantics, wellformedness/acceptance, a relation to
   the lower layer, compiler/lowering, and preservation theorem. You can add slices
   to that layer one at a time, but the layer needs to be feature-complete,
   not a toy version of the language, before moving on. Its feature set should
   cover the whole abstraction that belongs at that layer and, as far as possible
   before higher abstractions exist, match how that feature works in the source
   language being targeted.
   The semantics must be an independent interpreter or evaluation relation over
   that layer's own syntax. Defining the layer's run/eval as "lower/compile this
   program, then run the lower layer" is not a valid source semantics, except for
   an explicitly named transparent adapter boundary with no new source constructs
   and a recorded audit note.
   The semantics must also abstract the feature this layer introduces. Do not
   define a new source construct by exposing the lower representation it is meant
   to hide. For example, a locals/frame layer should have a named-environment
   source semantics; stack slots, layout depths, swaps, pops, or frame encodings
   belong in that layer's compiler/lowering relation and proof, not in the
   source interpreter used by higher layers.
5. Compose the new theorem into the public spine.
6. Run a layer audit gate before moving on.
7. Only then add the next layer.

Example of good abstraction steps include labels over byte offsets, structured control over
jumps, locals/frames over stack slots, expressions over primitive stack code,
functions over entry labels, or objects/modules over flat functions.

Bad layers are story-shaped features (`let-if-assign-return`), parser fixtures,
one-off combinations (`if` inside `for`), or helper representations with no
independent semantic contract.

Before implementing a broad layer, run this checklist. This is a thinking
checkpoint, not a request to create new documents:

- Grammar frozen: every construct in scope is named, and every tempting
  construct out of scope is explicitly excluded.
- Prior art checked: inspect the existing lower layer, adjacent completed
  layers, and any sibling worktree or earlier implementation the user points to
  before inventing a new proof route. Reuse proven theorem shapes when they
  fit; record why they do not if you diverge.
- Semantics frozen: outcomes, errors, effects, divergence/fuel behavior, and
  observable state are clear for the accepted subset.
- Interpreter independence checked: `run`/`Eval` is not merely lower-layer
  execution after compiling/elaborating the source; any exception is an explicit
  transparent adapter boundary, not a completed compiler layer.
- Abstraction boundary checked: the layer's source semantics hides the lower
  representation that its new feature abstracts. Any proof terms, layouts,
  slots, continuations, frame encodings, return tokens, cleanup code, or other
  lower-level machinery needed to implement the feature live in the compiler
  and preservation proof, not in the source interpreter or the interface used by
  higher layers.
- Lower capabilities pass through: the layer does not silently shrink the
  already-verified lower language surface.
- Accepted restrictions classified: every nontrivial `Accepted`/`WF` predicate
  is checked against the requested scope. An explicit predicate name is not by
  itself a justification; if it excludes lower-layer behavior because the proof
  route or representation is unfinished, keep the layer incomplete unless the
  user explicitly narrowed the language.
- Public theorem sketched: adjacent theorem and composed theorem have the right
  shape before helper proofs begin.
- Proof interface sketched: layout, freshness, state relation, continuation,
  resource, or environment assumptions are bundled when they are conceptually
  one invariant.
- Temporary scaffolds named: replay/certificate/helper routes have a planned
  replacement theorem or are kept private.
- Public certificate boundary checked: if a theorem still takes a compiler
  certificate, layout witness, replay witness, proof-carrying emitted-code
  segment, or generated-label table as an input, do not call the pass complete
  unless that certificate is itself generated by a checked compiler theorem or
  the user explicitly accepted it as a trusted input format.
- No public call oracle: for recursive source features, the public theorem must
  not take an all-callees-preserve, all-functions-preserve, replay, or call
  obligation premise. Discharge those obligations by source-fuel, evaluation,
  or well-founded induction, leaving only explicit resource bounds or source
  acceptedness assumptions at the public boundary.
- Public theorem grep: before declaring success, search the public spine for
  names like `Certificate`, `CompilationCertificate`, `Replay`, `Obligation`,
  `ProcPreserves`, `Layout`, `Evidence`, `CallPreserves`, and project-specific
  certificate names. Any remaining public occurrence must be either generated by
  a checked constructor theorem or justified as a fundamental resource/input
  premise in the audit entry.

## Source-Language Completeness

When the user asks for a verified compiler for a named source language or layer,
the default obligation is the complete semantics of that source language layer.
`Accepted`/`WF` may reject malformed, ill-scoped, ill-typed, or otherwise
semantically invalid programs, but it must not reject implemented source
constructs merely because they are proof-inconvenient unless the user explicitly
approved a fragment.

Before marking such a goal complete:

1. Inventory the source grammar against the source semantics and compiler.
2. For every construct, record one status: supported and covered by the theorem;
   semantically invalid and rejected by WF/Accepted; or explicitly out of scope
   by user-approved fragment boundary. Apply the same classification to every
   `Accepted`/`WF` field, not only to syntax constructors.
3. If the source is a named external or imported language, name the exact
   reference semantics being targeted and require a checked theorem from that
   semantics to the compiler source semantics; elaboration through the compiler
   is not enough by itself.
4. Confirm the source semantics is an independent interpreter or evaluation
   relation over the source syntax. If `run`/`Eval` delegates through `compile`,
   `lower`, `elaborate`, `toLower?`, or similar, the layer is incomplete until
   it has its own semantics and a checked equivalence/preservation theorem, or
   the user explicitly accepts it as a transparent adapter boundary.
5. Check that supported constructs include all outcomes their source semantics
   admits, including errors, halts, resource failures, divergence/fuel behavior,
   traces, and external observations claimed by the theorem.
6. Confirm theorem statements quantify over the real source semantics, not only
   over a compiler-success witness or replay certificate.
7. If any source construct is missing semantics or theorem coverage, keep
   working or report a blocker; do not call the compiler fully verified.

Add this source-language audit as its own `audit` entry in `PROGRESS_LOG.md` at
major layer boundaries and before declaring an end-to-end theorem complete.

Share source and target components where this reduces real proof burden:
values, arithmetic, memory/storage models, errors, traces, environments, and
external state. Do not share away the compiler obligation. Source and target
control semantics, layout, resource assumptions, and observations must remain
explicit.

It is valid for shared primitive operations to pass through the same semantics
across many layers when they are not the abstraction being introduced by that
layer. For example, arithmetic, hashing, memory/storage operations, and
explicitly shared external effects may reuse the same primitive meaning all the
way up to the source language. That exception does not apply to a feature whose
purpose is to hide a lower representation: locals should hide stack slots,
structured control should hide jump encodings, functions should hide
return-token/frame conventions, and so on.

## Layer Audit Gate

At the end of every semantic layer, pause and audit before adding the next
higher layer. This is a smaller recurring version of the completion gate, aimed
at catching theorem-boundary drift while the layer is still cheap to repair.

For the layer just finished:

1. Name the adjacent preservation theorem and the composed public spine theorem
   it feeds.
2. Check that syntax, semantics, acceptance/WF, lowering, relation, and
   observation/outcome model are all explicit for the whole accepted layer.
3. Check that the whole feature set belonging to this abstraction layer is
   implemented and proved, not just a narrow example slice. The feature set
   should be source-language-faithful to the extent possible at this layer,
   without smuggling in abstractions that properly belong to higher layers.
4. No silent narrowing: every lower-layer capability intended to reach the
   source language must pass through this layer; do not shrink the verified path
   to arithmetic-only or other convenient fragments. Audit the actual
   `Accepted`/`WF` predicates used by the public theorem; named safety predicates
   that exclude supported lower behavior still count as narrowing.
5. Verify the layer is conservative over the lower layer except for the single
   abstraction it introduces.
6. Verify abstraction ownership: the source semantics and public theorem surface
   for this layer must not expose the lower representation that the layer was
   created to abstract. If such representation concepts appear in public
   premises or outcomes, classify each occurrence as either a fundamental
   semantic observation, a shared primitive pass-through, or a leak that belongs
   in the compiler/preservation proof below the layer.
7. Run the narrowest meaningful build for the layer, and `#print axioms` or the
   local equivalent for its public theorem(s) when practical.
8. Scan the layer's public path for `sorry`, `admit`, `axiom`, `unsafe`,
   `partial`, obsolete fixture/story routes, and fused combo-case proofs.
9. Record one `audit` entry in `PROGRESS_LOG.md` with theorem names, command
   run, axiom result, and any remaining assumptions or unsupported behavior.

If the audit finds a shortcut, architecture risk, stale public route, or
accepted feature outside theorem coverage, fix or explicitly narrow the layer.
If the layer's feature set is too small for the abstraction it claims to own,
finish that layer before starting the next one.

## Preservation Shape

The main public theorem for an adjacent pass is a same-observation theorem.
Replay certificates, traces, and local simulations are proof machinery; they
should not be the public theorem boundary once the layer is stable.

Use this shape, adapted to local names:

```lean
theorem compile_sound
    (hWF : Hi.WF program)
    (hCompile : Hi.compile program = lower)
    (hEval : Hi.Eval program initial obs)
    (hRel : StateRel initial lowerInitial) :
    Exists fun lowerObs =>
      And (Lo.Eval lower lowerInitial lowerObs) (ObsRel obs lowerObs) := by
  ...
```

When both semantics are executable and deterministic, this may be an equality
theorem over `run`; when the layer erases representation details, use `ObsRel`.
The important claim is that the lower semantics has the same observable program
result, not merely that some hand-written replay witness exists.

Prefer strengthened, compositional theorem statements from the beginning.

Lean theorem boundaries matter. If witness data is derived from a `Prop`
relation such as a source run, evaluation derivation, or preservation theorem,
the public result should usually expose `∃` or `Nonempty` evidence. Do not make
the public route depend on returning an arbitrary structure in `Type` unless
that structure is produced by computation or is passed in as explicit data.

For expression-like code generation, use an arbitrary continuation/suffix:

```lean
theorem compile_correct_aux (e : Expr) (k : Code) (s : Stack) :
    run (compile e ++ k) s = run k (eval e :: s) := by
  induction e generalizing k s with
  | ... => ...
```

For statement/control layers, generalize this idea. Use whichever local shape
matches the layer:

- arbitrary code suffix;
- continuation or defunctionalized continuation;
- evaluation/control context;
- entry/destination labels;
- layout and no-wrap assumptions;
- state relation at an exact target PC, such as `RelAt`;
- outcome relation for normal return, halt, revert, throw, break/continue, or
  other abrupt exits.

The public proof route should be structural: sequence, context, branch, loop,
call, frame/layout, and outcome lemmas compose into the same-observation theorem.
If theorem names start encoding whole programs or feature combinations, stop and
replace them with generic recursive/compositional theorems.

If a proof is becoming a long run of nearly identical constructors or opcodes,
pause before continuing. Look for a semantic-family classifier, pass-through
lemma, source syntax traversal, or relation-preservation theorem that proves the
common case once and leaves only genuinely distinct cases as wrappers.

After a few helper lemmas for a new construct, inspect the next theorem
statement. If it needs many independent PC, label, freshness, layout, resource,
or environment premises, introduce a small structure or relation that names that
interface. Long premise lists are usually missing abstraction, not proof
progress.

Wherever feasible, derive full preservation proofs from accepted source runs;
treat assumed replay/certificate witnesses as temporary scaffolding, not the
public theorem boundary.

Compiler-generated evidence is not a fundamental assumption. Before declaring a
layer done, try to prove a checked constructor for every public certificate:
layout, freshness, label resolution, call-site table inclusion, PC-fit, typed
continuation boundary, and compiler-output equality. If construction is not yet
proved, the layer is not complete; log the missing constructor and keep working
or explicitly report the blocker.

Do not hide unfinished compiler evidence inside source acceptance. `Accepted`
may bundle source wellformedness, source semantic safety, checked resource
limits, or user-approved trusted-input contracts, but it must not contain a
compiler-generated layout, replay witness, call-site table, label-resolution
proof, procedure-body preservation proof, or semantic call oracle unless the
skill user explicitly chose proof-carrying source input as the trusted source
format. If a preservation theorem needs such evidence, either generate it with
a checked compiler theorem or keep the layer incomplete.

For recursive source features such as procedure calls, function calls,
recursive loops expressed through fuel, or mutually recursive declarations, the
default discharge route is induction on source fuel or on the relational
evaluation derivation. Do not replace this with an assumed "all callees
preserve" oracle. If a temporary all-callee/call obligation is introduced, keep
it private, give it a fuel-bounded replacement plan immediately, and do not
report the layer complete until the public theorem derives it.

Avoid brittle fusion lemmas. A lemma about `if` inside `loop`, `switch` inside
`for`, or assignment plus branch plus return is not a milestone unless it is a
private stepping stone being replaced immediately by generic `seq`/`if`/`switch`
`loop`/`outcome` composition. If a fused lemma remains useful, log it as a
`shortcut` or `architecture-risk` and keep it out of the public spine.

CPS is a tool, not a mandate. Raw higher-order continuations can make Lean
terms huge. Prefer a small continuation/context interface that keeps compiled
programs folded and lets induction hypotheses apply under arbitrary suffixes.

## Accepted Subsets

Full preservation means full semantics for the accepted subset, but an accepted
subset is allowed only when the user requested a fragment or when the source
language definition itself is intentionally smaller than its parser or host AST.
If the user asks for a compiler for the whole source language, the accepted
subset must be source-complete except for malformed or semantically invalid
programs.

Do prove all relevant outcomes of accepted programs: success, errors, halts,
resource failures, traces, divergence/fuel behavior, and external observations
that the theorem claims to model.

Do not prove only the terminating happy path unless the theorem name and
accepted checker explicitly say that is the claim. Unsupported behavior should
be rejected by `Accepted`/`WF`, guarded by explicit theorem assumptions, or
called executable-only.

Keep these notions separate:

- parser/decoder success;
- semantic acceptance or wellformedness;
- compiler success;
- certificate checking;
- target execution success.

Accepted input must not mean "the compiler returned `some`." Compiler-success
theorems are useful, but they are weaker than accepted-input theorems.

## Lean Blowup Rules

Treat timeouts and heartbeat explosions as architecture feedback, not merely
tactic problems.

Do not let Lean normalize whole compiled programs as a proof strategy.

## Context Hygiene

Preserve context for theorem state, not logs or repo tours:

- Before every read, search, or build, name the narrow question it should
  answer; avoid fresh "getting bearings" sweeps after a handoff identifies the
  next target.
- Keep build output out of context: redirect noisy `lake build` logs to `/tmp`
  and inspect only `error:` lines plus the smallest needed neighborhood.
- Scope searches tightly. Prefer module-specific `rg`, `rg -n -m`,
  `rg --files`, `git diff --stat`, and short line windows; broad repo-wide
  `rg`, full diffs, generated-file searches, and wide `sed` ranges are last
  resorts.
- On resume, trust the latest handoff/progress log unless a specific line must
  be checked.
- If the user explicitly allows subagents for large read-only searches or
  audits, consume their summaries rather than raw match dumps.
- After any large tool or subagent output, retain only theorem names, file/line
  pointers, failing goals, and the concrete next patch.

Prefer:

- structural lemmas over syntax/control contexts;
- one-step semantic interface lemmas;
- semantic classifiers for large opcode/operator families;
- small public wrapper theorems around imported or recursive definitions;
- explicit state/layout relations instead of massive record equalities;
- named intermediate definitions to share structure;
- `simp only [...]` with local simp sets;
- controlled unfolding of one definition at a time;
- narrow module builds: `lake build Module.Name` or `lake env lean path/File.lean`.
- recursive theorem families whose structurally decreasing syntax argument comes
  early in the argument list, with `termination_by` added before the proof grows.

Avoid:

- broad `simp_all` over compiler and interpreter definitions;
- unfolding imported dispatchers across many constructors;
- one theorem that case-splits over a large instruction set and tries many
  `first | change ...` branches;
- exposing large recursive compiler definitions as global simp rules;
- proof terms that inline every compiled instruction or generated label;
- broad imports in theorem files;
- adding local heartbeats before checking whether the theorem/interface shape is
  wrong.
- continuing a proof whose statement has become a page of plumbing. Bundle the
  invariant and prove the compiler supplies it.

When widening primitive operations, classify by semantic family or require a
small proof-carrying/accepted primitive interface. Prove PC/resource/state
insensitivity once per family, then use a one-line wrapper per constructor. Do
not ask Lean to rediscover the same dispatcher facts for every opcode.

## Primitive Classifiers

For large primitive or opcode surfaces, introduce a small semantic-family API
before broadening the source layer. This API should be a proof boundary, not a
second unverified semantics.


## Documentation And Logs

Code and theorem statements are the source of truth. Before reporting status,
inspect the actual theorem names, statements, public imports, and build output.

`ROADMAP.md` should stay sparse:

```markdown
# Roadmap

## Public Spine

Accepted AST -> LayerA -> LayerB -> Target interpreter

## Next Layer

- [ ] Interface: syntax, semantics, WF, relation
- [ ] Complete source-faithful feature set for this layer
- [ ] Lowering function
- [ ] Adjacent same-observation theorem
- [ ] Composed public theorem
- [ ] Layer audit gate
```

`PROGRESS_LOG.md` is append-only and flat:

```markdown
- 2026-05-12 17:09:35 - oracle - received critique for `...`; disposition accepted: arbitrary-initial-PC theorem is false; use `RelAt`.
- 2026-05-12 18:17:26 - proof - proved `CompilerPreservation.block` and `compile_whole_program_sound_of_run`; command `lake build`; result green.
- 2026-05-12 18:20:00 - architecture-risk - primitive widening proof unfolds full opcode dispatcher; replace with semantic family interface before adding more ops.
```

Use tags such as `proof`, `test`, `audit`, `oracle`, `bottleneck`,
`architecture-risk`, `shortcut`, `consolidation`, `deletion`, and `incident`.
For risks and shortcuts, name the artifact, why it is risky, and the generic
theorem/interface that should replace it.

Keep logs current, not just append-heavy. When a bottleneck, shortcut, or risk
is resolved or superseded, add a short entry saying so and name the replacing
theorem or interface. Do not leave stale warnings that still read as active.

## Git Preservation

Use git to preserve meaningful theorem-bearing states. Commit only coherent
milestones, preferably green:

- initial Lean package setup;
- first target-reaching theorem;
- new public layer or theorem boundary;
- accepted-language/theorem-boundary change;
- byte encoder or real-machine bridge;
- deletion of obsolete fixture/story routes;
- audited stable proof milestone.

Never revert user changes. Before pausing or finishing substantial work, run
`git status --short` and make the handoff state clear.

## Oracle Use

Use `oracle` for theorem-boundary critique, hard invariant design, suspected
false statements, and Lean architecture traps. Do not use it for routine syntax
or small tactic cleanup.

Ask broad hostile critiques at major layer boundaries or before declaring a
feature track complete. Ask narrow questions for blocked proofs. Record only
conversation/response IDs and the disposition in `PROGRESS_LOG.md`.

Package enough context for independent critique: theorem statements, semantics,
relations, accepted predicates, current public spine, build/axiom results,
failed proof shape, and what would count as useful failure.

## Anti-Patterns

Stop and repair the architecture if any of these appear:

- full high-level language first, proofs later;
- theorem ends at an IR while the claim says end-to-end;
- special theorems for `if` inside `loop` or other combinations;
- fused feature lemmas become public proof routes instead of temporary private
  scaffolding;
- parser helper recognizes a whole story instead of independent constructs;
- semantic classifier or helper interpreter used as if it were the real target
  without an equality/refinement theorem;
- source semantics changed to match a compiler bug;
- broad public imports retain obsolete compiler routes;
- proof relies on `sorry`, `admit`, new `axiom`, `unsafe`, `partial`, or
  proof-critical external assumptions without excluding them from the claim;
- tests or oracle advice are treated as verification;
- Lean timeout is answered by adding more feature code.

## Completion Gate

Do not call the compiler verified because tests pass, the compiler runs, or a
scaffold theorem exists.

Before reporting a verified milestone:

1. Inspect the accepted compiler path.
2. Name the exact top theorem(s).
3. Run the narrowest meaningful build command, and full build when practical.
4. Run `#print axioms` or the local equivalent on public top theorem(s) when
   practical.
5. Scan for `sorry`, `admit`, `axiom`, `unsafe`, and `partial`.
6. Check public imports for obsolete fixture/story/legacy routes.
7. Check public theorem arguments for compiler-generated certificates or layout
   evidence. They must be discharged by checked constructors, be private helper
   inputs, or be explicitly named as trusted external inputs approved by the
   user. Otherwise keep working.
8. Inspect `Accepted`/`WF` records used by the public theorem. They must not
   smuggle in compiler-output equality, label layout, replay certificates,
   call/return layout, generated-token uniqueness, or semantic preservation
   oracles. They also must not exclude lower-layer capabilities merely because
   the representation or proof is unfinished. If they do, split those fields out
   and discharge them, explicitly narrow the requested source language with the
   user, or keep the milestone incomplete.
9. State remaining assumptions and unsupported features plainly.

The goal is complete only when every source-language feature in the requested
scope has a checked path from trusted input or AST through acceptance,
semantics, compiler/lowering, target interpreter, and theorem. If a fragment was
explicitly requested, say so in the theorem names or surrounding API and audit
the fragment boundary. Otherwise report the current work as a theorem-bearing
milestone and keep working on the missing source semantics.

## References

Load only when useful:

- `references/verified-compiler-patterns.md`: theorem-boundary patterns and
  classic verified-compiler references.
- `references/process-lessons.md`: earlier process failures to avoid.

</skill>
````
